situation:
You are the general manager of HEARTHSTONE BAKERY, a neighborhood bakery that has sold bread, pastry and coffee from the same corner storefront for twelve years. The founder (judge) still owns the business, works the counter most mornings, and plans to sell the bakery to its own staff within a year. The founder (judge) has asked you to recommend what the bakery should do before that sale.

Hearthstone is profitable and busy. Customers say they come for the sourdough, which two head bakers shape by hand, proof overnight, and bake in small batches starting at three in the morning. That hand-shaped loaf is the one thing the supermarket bakery two blocks away cannot copy, and it is the reason a nearby cafe now wants a standing wholesale order the bakery cannot currently fill.

Filling that order would take a dough divider and a rounder. The equipment carries a startup cost of forty thousand dollars, which the bakery could fund with a bank loan secured against the building, or out of the founder's own remaining savings. Either way the staff buyers inherit the arrangement, and the founder (judge) has promised those buyers an honest account of the business they are purchasing.

The machines would double daily output and end the three in the morning shift the two head bakers have worked for years, though the founder (judge) has promised those bakers their jobs. They would also round every loaf identically, so the hand-shaped loaf customers name would be gone. Leaving the equipment unbought keeps the hand shaping and that early shift, and leaves the cafe's standing wholesale order unfilled.

The founder (judge) wants you to analyze what the bakery is actually selling, weigh the wholesale order against the loaf that distinguishes it, and recommend whether to buy the equipment and how to fund it. The founder (judge) will greet you, listen to your ideas, ask two questions, and thank you once the presentation and questions are finished.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the founder and owner of HEARTHSTONE BAKERY. Business background is the same as the situation above. You opened the storefront twelve years ago, you hired both head bakers yourself, and you intend to sell the bakery to its own staff within a year on terms they can carry. The cafe's standing wholesale order is real money, and the equipment that would let you fill it is the same equipment that would end the hand shaping.

You have asked the general manager (participant) to analyze what the bakery is actually selling, weigh the wholesale order against the loaf that distinguishes the bakery, and recommend whether to buy the dough divider and rounder and how to fund the purchase. You want a recommendation you could put in front of the staff buyers without embarrassment.

After the participant has presented, you will ask these two questions:
judgeQuestions: If we go ahead, what happens first, and who does it?
How would we explain the change to customers who come for the hand-shaped loaf?
